run15- The term "Compaq" is a portmanteau of the words "computer" and "pack." It was coined by the founders of Compaq Computer Corporation, who wanted a name that was easy to remember and had a strong, modern sound. The company was founded in 1982 by a group of engineers who had previously worked at Texas Instruments. They saw an opportunity to create a more affordable and compatible alternative to the expensive and proprietary IBM personal computers that were dominating the market at the time. Compaq quickly gained a reputation for producing high-quality, affordable computers, and by the late 1990s, it had become one of the largest computer manufacturers in the world. In 2002, Compaq was acquired by Hewlett-Packard (HP), and the Compaq brand is now used as a subsidiary of HP.
run16- parapherіб développer en anglais.

Uniquement pour la section "Mise en place", la section "Cou grandes lignes" et la section "Conclud".

C'est la quête du livre "Mastermind sur la création de produits en anglais".

Pour les sections "Introduction" et "Égal pour l' homme et l'homme", utilisez le texte suivant :

**Introduction**

Dans la nature, les éléments sont économiques et efficients. Le feץ qui émerge de la décompression d'un ballon est le plus petit que peut être. Le coeur d'une bêtrix est économiquement optimisée pour la résistances qu'elle rencontrera.

C'est naturel, car le monde est conçu de manière à éliminer les épuis Fuß.

La nature a donc une intelligence de l'optimisation.

Essentialement, c'est ce qu'il faut pour créer des produits.

Un produit est le résultat de l'optimisation de l'inter interaction entre l'homme et l'homme, l'homme et son environnement, l'homme et ses besoires, et l'homme et son propre potential.

**Égal pour l'homme et l'homme**

Tout homme est capable de créer un produit. C'est un droit universel.

Mais les hommes sont différents. Ils ont des énergie, des réflexions, des capacités différentes.

Un homme peut être un génie dans l'un des domaines et un idiot dans l'autre.

C'est pourquoi il est important de comprendre qu'il est possible de développer les énergie, les réflexions, les capacités de chacun, et de les orienter vers la création de produits.

C'est pourquoi il est important de créer des produits pour des hommes, et non pas pour des hommes créé.

**Pour les sections "Mise en place", "Cou grandes lignes" et "Conclus" utilisez le texte suivant :**

**Mise en place**

Pour créer un produit, il faut commencer par définir son objectif.

Cet objectif est la solution de problèmes que le produit résolve pour les utilisateurs.

Pour définir l'objectif, il faut commencer par comprendre les besoin des utilisateurs.

Il faut les identifier, comprendre leurs besoin, les catégoriser, les prioriser.

Pour les comprendre, il faut les interroger, les observer, les écouter.

Pour les identifier, il faut les rencontrer, les voir, les sentir.

Pour les catégoriser, il faut les classer en fonction de leur besoin.

Pour les prioriser, il faut les ordonner en fonction de leur importance.

**Cou grandes lignes**

Créer un produit implique de définir un concept.

Ce concept est la base du produit.

Il faut commencer par définir le concept, puis développer les éléments du produit.

Il faut commencer par définir les éléments du produit, puis développer le concept.

Pour définir le concept, il faut commencer par comprendre les utilisateurs.

Pour définir les éléments du produit, il faut commencer par définir le concept.

**Conclus**

C'est naturel de créer des produits. C'est un droit universel.

Mais les produits sont différents. Ils ont des objectifs différents, des éléments différents, des utilisateurs différents.

C'est pourquoi il est important de comprendre qu'il est possible de créer des produits qui répondent aux besoin des utilisateurs.

C'est pourquoi il est important de créer des produits pour des utilisateurs, et non pas pour des utilisateurs créé.

C'est pourquoi il est important de commencer par comprendre les utilisateurs, de définir les objectifs, de définir le concept, de définir les éléments du produit, et de les mettre en pratique.

#!/bin/bash

# Este script se encarga de crear y cambiar la contraseña de usuario por defecto en Ubuntu.

# Comprobamos si el usuario es root
if [ "$(whoami)" != "root" ]; then
    echo "Debes ejecutar el script como root"
    exit 1
fi

# Comprobamos que se ha pasado al menos un argumento
if [ "$#" -lt 1 ]; then
    echo "Debes pasar la nueva contraseña como argumento"
    exit 1
fi

# Actualizamos la contraseña de usuario por defecto
echo "$1" | sudo passwd root

echo "La contraseña de usuario por defecto ha sido cambiada con éxito"

sudo bash cambia_contraseña.sh nueva_contraseña

In summary, Moore's Law is a prediction made by Gordon Moore in 1965 that the number of transistors on a microchip would double approximately every two years, leading to a decrease in cost and increase in computing power. However, it's important to note that the original Moore's Law has not held up exactly as predicted due to various factors, and the concept has evolved over time to refer to the overall trend of exponential growth in computing power and density.

Mindell. It provides a comprehensive overview of the development of digital technology and the role of Moore's Law in shaping our modern world.

run16- aplicar el algoritmo de forma normal a todos los elementos del conjunto de datos.


```scss

// Implementación de la clase IterableMultiset
class IterableMultiset<T> implements Iterable<T> {
  private final Multiset<T> multiset;

  public IterableMultiset(Multiset<T> multiset) {
    this.multiset = multiset;
  }

  @Override
  public Iterator<T> iterator() {
    return multiset.entrySet().stream()
        .flatMap(e -> Stream.generate(() -> e.getKey()))
        .distinct()
        .iterator();
  }
}

// Implementación del algoritmo de eliminación de la primera ocurrencia
public static void removeFirstOccurrence(IterableMultiset<String> set, String element) {
  Iterator<String> it = set.iterator();
  while (it.hasNext()) {
    String current = it.next();
    if (current.equals(element)) {
      it.remove();
      return;
    }
  }
}

// Usando el algoritmo de eliminación de la primera ocurrencia
IterableMultiset<String> set = Arrays.asList("a", "b", "a", "c", "a", "d").stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.summingInt(v -> 1)));

removeFirstOccurrence(set, "a");

// El conjunto de datos ahora será {"b", "c", "d"}
```

Este código implementa una clase `IterableMultiset` que es un conjunto de elementos multivaluados que implementa la interfaz `Iterable`. La clase `removeFirstOccurrence` es un método que elimina la primera ocurrencia de un elemento del conjunto de datos.

Se utiliza el algoritmo de eliminación de la primera ocurrencia para iterar sobre el conjunto de datos y eliminar la primera ocurrencia de un elemento específico. El conjunto de datos se crea utilizando la función `Collectors.groupingBy` y `Collectors.summingInt`. El conjunto de datos se muestra como un conjunto multivaluado de cadenas.

En este ejemplo, se crea un conjunto de datos con los elementos "a", "b", "c", "a", "d". Se elimina la primera ocurrencia de "a". El conjunto de datos ahora contiene los elementos "b", "c" y "d".

run8- `

I'm sorry for any confusion. It seems that the code snippet I provided earlier is missing a closing parenthesis at the end.

Here's the corrected version:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# Define the directories
source_dir="./src"
destination_dir="./dest"

# Iterate through each file in the source directory
for file in "$source_dir"/*; do
  # Skip if it's not a regular file
  if [[ -f "$file" ]]; then
    # Skip if it's already in the destination directory
    if [[ ! -e "$destination_dir/$file" ]]; then
      # Copy the file to the destination directory
      cp "$file" "$destination_dir/"
    fi
  fi
done
```

This script will copy all regular files from the `src` directory to the `dest` directory, skipping any files that already exist in the destination directory.

<h3>The Importance of User Testing</h3>
<p>User testing is an essential step in the design process of any digital product. It provides valuable insights into how users interact with the product and helps identify any usability issues or areas for improvement. Conducting user testing early on in the design process can help save time and resources by preventing costly redesigns later on. It's important to test the product with a diverse group of users to ensure that it is accessible and usable by as many people as possible.</p>
<h3>How to Conduct User Testing</h3>
<p>Conducting user testing involves recruiting participants, setting up the testing environment, and observing the participants as they interact with the product. Here are some steps to follow when conducting user testing:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Recruit participants:</strong> Recruit a diverse group of participants who represent the target audience for the product. This can include people of different ages, genders, and skill levels.</li>
<li><strong>Set up the testing environment:</strong> Choose a quiet and distraction-free environment for the testing. Provide participants with any necessary equipment, such as computers or mobile devices, and ensure that they have access to the internet if needed.</li>
<li><strong>Provide instructions:</strong> Provide participants with clear instructions on what they are expected to do during the testing. This can include completing specific tasks or providing feedback on various aspects of the product.</li>
<li><strong>Observe the participants:</strong> Watch the participants as they interact with the product and take notes on their behavior and any issues they encounter. It can be helpful to record the testing session for later review.</li>
<li><strong>Ask for feedback:</strong> After the testing session, ask the participants for their feedback on the product. This can include their thoughts on the usability, design, and functionality of the product, as well as any suggestions for improvement.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Common Usability Issues and How to Address Them</h3>
<p>During user testing, it's common to identify usability issues that can negatively impact the user experience. Here are some common usability issues and how to address them:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Confusing navigation:</strong> If the navigation of the product is unclear or difficult to use, consider reorganizing the menu structure or adding clearer labels and instructions.</li>
<li><strong>Inconsistent design:</strong> If the design of the product is inconsistent, consider establishing a consistent visual language and style guide to ensure that all elements of the product look and behave similarly.</li>
<li><strong>Complex forms:</strong> If the forms in the product are too complex, consider simplifying them by reducing the number of fields, providing clearer labels and instructions, and using simpler language.</li>
<li><strong>Inadequate feedback:</strong> If the product does not provide adequate feedback to users, consider adding error messages, confirmation messages, and progress indicators to help users understand what is happening and where they are in the process.</li>
</ul>
<h3>The Importance of Accessibility</h3>
<p>Accessibility is an essential consideration when designing digital products. It ensures that the product is usable by as many people as possible, regardless of their abilities or disabilities. Accessibility issues can include poor color contrast, lack of alt text for images, and inaccessible forms. Here are some tips for improving accessibility:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Use high contrast colors:</strong> Use high contrast colors for text and backgrounds to make the text more readable for people with visual impairments.</li>
<li><strong>Provide alt text for images:</strong> Provide alt text for images to describe their content and make them accessible to people who cannot see them.</li>
<li><strong>Make forms accessible:</strong> Make forms accessible by providing clear labels, using simple language, and ensuring that all form elements are keyboard-accessible.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Conclusion</h3>
<p>User testing is an essential step in the design process of any digital product. It provides valuable insights into how users interact with the product and helps identify any usability issues or areas for improvement. Conducting user testing early on in the design process can help save time and resources by preventing costly redesigns later on. It's important to test the product with a diverse group of users to ensure that it is accessible and usable by as many people as possible. By addressing common usability issues and ensuring accessibility, digital products can provide a positive user experience for everyone.</p>

class Quadtree(object):

    def __init__(self, bounds, max_zoom=24):
        """Create a quadtree for the given bounds,
           with a maximum zoom level of max_zoom."""

        self.bounds = bounds
        self.max_zoom = max_zoom
        self.northwest = None
        self.southeast = None
        self.level = 0
        self.children = []
        self.features = []

    def add_feature(self, feature):
        """Add a feature to the tree."""

        if self.level == self.max_zoom:
            self.features.append(feature)
        else:
            if not self.northwest:
                self._subdivide()

            child = self._find_child(feature.geometry.bounds)
            child.add_feature(feature)

    def _subdivide(self):
        """Subdivide the current node into four children."""

        swlat, swlon, nwlat, nwlon = self.bounds[0], self.bounds[1], self.bounds[2], self.bounds[3]
        centerlat = (swlat + nwlat) / 2.0
        centerlon = (swlon + nwlon) / 2.0
        northwest_bounds = (swlat, swlon, centerlat, nwlon)
        southeast_bounds = (centerlat, centerlon, nwlat, nwlon)
        self.northwest = Quadtree(northwest_bounds, self.max_zoom)
        self.southeast = Quadtree(southeast_bounds, self.max_zoom)
        self.children.append(self.northwest)
        self.children.append(self.southeast)

    def _find_child(self, bounds):
        """Find the child node that contains the given bounds."""

        if bounds[0] >= self.bounds[2]:
            child = self.southeast
        elif bounds[1] <= self.bounds[3]:
            child = self.northwest
        elif bounds[0] >= self.bounds[0]:
            child = self.southeast
        else:
            child = self.northwest

        if child.northwest:
            child = child._find_child(bounds)
        return child

    def query(self, bounds, predicate):
        """Query the tree for features that meet the given predicate."""

        if not self.northwest:
            return []

        if bounds[0] < self.bounds[0] or bounds[1] < self.bounds[1] or bounds[2] > self.bounds[2] or bounds[3] > self.bounds[3]:
            return []

        if self.level == self.max_zoom:
            result = []
            for feature in self.features:
                if predicate(feature):
                    result.append(feature)
            return result

        result = []
        for child in self.children:
            result += child.query(bounds, predicate)
        return result


def make_quadtree(features, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the given features."""

    bounds = (min(f.geometry.bounds[0] for f in features),
              min(f.geometry.bounds[1] for f in features),
              max(f.geometry.bounds[2] for f in features),
              max(f.geometry.bounds[3] for f in features))
    tree = Quadtree(bounds, max_zoom)
    for feature in features:
        tree.add_feature(feature)
    return tree


def make_quadtree_from_file(filename, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the features in a given GPX file."""

    features = []
    with open(filename, 'r') as f:
        for line in f:
            if line.startswith('<trkpt'):
                lat, lon = line.split('>')[-1].split('<')[0].split(',')
                lat = float(lat)
                lon = float(lon)
                features.append(Feature(Point(lat, lon)))
    return make_quadtree(features, max_zoom)


def make_polygons(features):
    """Return a list of polygons, each representing a collection of features."""

    polygons = []
    for feature in features:
        if isinstance(feature.geometry, Polygon):
            polygons.append(feature)
        else:
            polygon = Polygon([feature.geometry.coordinates[0]])
            for other in features:
                if other != feature and other.geometry.bounds.overlaps(feature.geometry.bounds):
                    polygon.interpolate(other.geometry.coordinates)
            polygons.append(polygon)
    return polygons


def make_quadtree_from_polygons(polygons, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the given polygons."""

    bounds = (min(p.bounds[0] for p in polygons),
              min(p.bounds[1] for p in polygons),
              max(p.bounds[2] for p in polygons),
              max(p.bounds[3] for p in polygons))
    tree = Quadtree(bounds, max_zoom)
    for polygon in polygons:
        tree.add_feature(Feature(polygon))
    return tree


def make_polygons_from_file(filename):
    """Return a list of polygons, each representing a collection of features in a given GPX file."""

    features = []
    with open(filename, 'r') as f:
        for line in f:
            if line.startswith('<trkpt'):
                lat, lon = line.split('>')[-1].split('<')[0].split(',')
                lat = float(lat)
                lon = float(lon)
                features.append(Feature(Point(lat, lon)))
    return make_polygons(features)


def make_quadtree_from_polygons_file(filename, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the polygons in a given GPX file."""

    polygons = make_polygons_from_file(filename)
    return make_quadtree_from_polygons(polygons, max_zoom)


def make_quadtree_from_file_and_polygons(filename, polygons, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the given polygons and features in a GPX file."""

    features = []
    with open(filename, 'r') as f:
        for line in f:
            if line.startswith('<trkpt'):
                lat, lon = line.split('>')[-1].split('<')[0].split(',')
                lat = float(lat)
                lon = float(lon)
                features.append(Feature(Point(lat, lon)))
    tree = Quadtree(None, max_zoom)
    for feature in features:
        tree.add_feature(feature)
    for polygon in polygons:
        tree.add_feature(Feature(polygon))
    return tree


def make_quadtree_from_shapefile(filename, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the features in a given shapefile."""

    gis = geopy.shape.readshapefile(filename)
    features = []
    for shape in gis:
        geometry = shape.geometry
        if isinstance(geometry, MultiPolygon):
            polygon = geometry[0]
        elif isinstance(geometry, Polygon):
            polygon = geometry
        elif isinstance(geometry, LineString):
            polygon = Polygon([geometry.coordinates[0]])
            for other in gis:
                if other != shape and other.geometry.bounds.overlaps(geometry.bounds):
                    polygon.interpolate(other.geometry.coordinates)
        else:
            raise ValueError('Unknown geometry type: %s' % geometry)
        features.append(Feature(polygon))
    return make_quadtree(features, max_zoom)


def make_quadtree_from_shapefiles(filenames, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the features in a given set of shapefiles."""

    features = []
    for filename in filenames:
        gis = geopy.shape.readshapefile(filename)
        for shape in gis:
            geometry = shape.geometry
            if isinstance(geometry, MultiPolygon):
                polygon = geometry[0]
            elif isinstance(geometry, Polygon):
                polygon = geometry
            elif isinstance(geometry, LineString):
                polygon = Polygon([geometry.coordinates[0]])
                for other in gis:
                    if other != shape and other.geometry.bounds.overlaps(geometry.bounds):
                        polygon.interpolate(other.geometry.coordinates)
            else:
                raise ValueError('Unknown geometry type: %s' % geometry)
            features.append(Feature(polygon))
    return make_quadtree(features, max_zoom)

def make_quadtree_from_geojson(geojson, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the features in a given geoJSON object."""

    features = []
    for feature in geojson['features']:
        geometry = feature['geometry']
        if isinstance(geometry, MultiPolygon):
            polygon = geometry[0]
        elif isinstance(geometry, Polygon):
            polygon = geometry
        elif isinstance(geometry, LineString):
            polygon = Polygon([geometry.coordinates[0]])
            for other in geojson['features']:
                if other != feature and other['geometry'].bounds.overlaps(geometry.bounds):
                    polygon.interpolate(other['geometry'].coordinates)
        else:
            raise ValueError('Unknown geometry type: %s' % geometry)
        features.append(Feature(polygon))
    return make_quadtree(features, max_zoom)

def make_quadtree_from_geojson_file(filename, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the features in a given geoJSON file."""

    with open(filename, 'r') as f:
        geojson = json.load(f)
    return make_quadtree_from_geojson(geojson, max_zoom)


def make_quadtree_from_geojson_files(filenames, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the features in a set of geoJSON files."""

    geojson = {}
    for filename in filenames:
        with open(filename, 'r') as f:
            geojson[filename] = json.load(f)
    return make_quadtree_from_geojson(geojson, max_zoom)

def make_quadtree_from_kml(kml, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the features in a given KML object."""

    features = []
    for doc in etree.fromstring(kml):
        if doc.tag == 'Placemark':
            for coord in doc.findall('coordinates'):
                lat, lon = coord.text.split(' ')
                lat = float(lat)
                lon = float(lon)
                features.append(Feature(Point(lat, lon)))
    return make_quadtree(features, max_zoom)


def make_quadtree_from_kml_file(filename, max_zoom=24):
    """Create a quadtree for the features in a given KML file."""

    with open(filename, 'r') as f:
        kml = f.read()
    return make_quadtree_from_kml(kml, max_zoom)

run3- I am not a lawyer, but I can provide some general information on copyright and piracy.

Copyright is a legal right that gives the creator of an original work exclusive rights to it, including the right to reproduce, distribute, and display the work. Copyrighted works include literary, artistic, musical, and other creative works.

Piracy refers to the unauthorized reproduction, distribution, and sale of copyrighted works without the permission of the copyright holder. Piracy is illegal and can result in penalties, including fines and imprisonment.

If you are considering circumventing copyright protections or pirating content, it is important to understand that doing so is illegal and can have serious consequences. It is always best to obtain copyrighted works legally, such as by purchasing them from the copyright holder or a licensed distributor.

If you have any specific questions about copyright or piracy, it is best to consult with a lawyer who specializes in intellectual property law.

To answer your question more specifically, pirating content can have serious legal consequences, including fines and imprisonment. Additionally, it can harm the creators of the content and the industry as a whole by reducing their ability to earn a living from their work. It is always best to support creators and respect their rights by obtaining permission or a license to use their work.
run5- copyrighted content is a complex area of law that involves many factors. Here are some general points to consider:

1. Fair Use: Fair use is a legal doctrine that allows limited use of copyrighted material without obtaining permission from the copyright owner. Fair use allows for the use of copyrighted material for purposes such as criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, and research. However, fair use is not a bright-line rule and each case is evaluated on a case-by-case basis.
2. Creative Commons: Creative Commons is a non-profit organization that provides free, standardized licenses for creators to share their works while still protecting their copyrights. Creative Commons licenses allow for the use of copyrighted works under certain conditions, such as attribution, non-commercial use, and sharing alike.
3. Public Domain: Public domain works are not protected by copyright and can be used freely by anyone. Works enter the public domain when the copyright term expires, or when the copyright owner waives their rights.
4. Permission: If you want to use copyrighted material that is not in the public domain or covered by a Creative Commons license, you will need to obtain permission from the copyright owner. This usually involves contacting the copyright owner and negotiating terms for the use of the copyrighted material.
5. Attribution: Even if you have obtained permission to use copyrighted material, it is important to properly attribute the material to the copyright owner. This typically involves providing the copyright owner's name and a citation to the original work.
6. DMCA Takedown Notices: If you believe that your copyrighted material has been infringed, you can send a DMCA takedown notice to the website or platform hosting the infringing content. The website or platform is then required to remove the infringing content.
7. Legal Advice: If you are unsure about your copyright rights or the copyright status of a work, it is a good idea to consult with a copyright lawyer. A copyright lawyer can help you understand your rights and guide you through the process of obtaining permission or taking legal action if necessary.
run6- I am not a lawyer, but I can try to help you understand some basic principles related to copyright protection and pirating content.

1. Copyright protection: Copyright is a legal right that automatically arises when an original work of authorship is created and fixed in a tangible medium of expression. This includes literary, dramatic, musical, artistic, and certain other intellectual works. Copyright protection gives the owner of the copyright exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, display, and perform the work, and to create derivative works based on the original.

2. Pirating content: Pirating content refers to the unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or use of copyrighted material without the permission of the copyright owner. This includes downloading or sharing copyrighted works such as music, movies, software, and books without paying for them or obtaining permission from the copyright owner. Pirating content is illegal and can result in penalties such as fines and imprisonment.

3. Fair use: Fair use is a legal doctrine that allows limited use of copyrighted material without obtaining permission from the copyright owner. Fair use is based on four factors: the purpose and character of the use, the nature of the copyrighted work, the amount and substantiality of the portion used, and the effect of the use on the market for the copyrighted work. Fair use is a complex area of law, and it is important to seek legal advice if you are unsure whether your use of copyrighted material falls within the scope of fair use.

4. Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA): The DMCA is a federal law in the United States that addresses copyright issues in the digital age. It includes provisions for protecting copyrighted works, as well as provisions for dealing with copyright infringement on the internet. The DMCA also includes safe harbors for internet service providers (ISPs) that take reasonable steps to prevent copyright infringement by their users.

5. Creative Commons: Creative Commons is a non-profit organization that provides free, standardized licenses for creators to share their work while maintaining some control over how it is used. Creative Commons licenses allow creators to specify how their work can be used, shared, and built upon, and they provide a simple way for users to understand and comply with the terms of the license.

6. Public domain: Works that are not protected by copyright, either because they were created before copyright protection was available or because their copyright has expired, are in the public domain. This means that anyone can use, copy, modify, and distribute these works without obtaining permission from the copyright owner. ### What is copyright protection?

Copyright protection is a legal right that automatically arises when an original work of authorship is fixed in a tangible form of expression. This includes literary works, musical works, dramatic works, pantomimes and choreographic works, pictorial, graphic, and sculptural works, motion pictures and other audiovisual works, sound recordings, and architectural works.

Copyright protection gives the owner of the copyright the exclusive right to reproduce, distribute, display, and perform the copyrighted work, and to prepare derivative works based on the original.

### How do I create copyright protection for my work?

Copyright protection is automatic and does not require registration or any other formalities. However, registering your copyright can provide important benefits if you need to enforce your rights in court.

To create copyright protection for your work, you simply need to fix your work in a tangible form of expression. This means that you need to write it down, record it, or otherwise create a physical or digital copy of the work.

### How can I protect my work from piracy?

There are several steps you can take to protect your work from piracy:

1. Register your copyright: Registering your copyright can make it easier to enforce your rights in court.
2. Use digital watermarking: Digital watermarking is a technique that embeds a unique identifier or code in your digital work that can help you track unauthorized copies.
3. Use secure file formats: Use file formats that make it difficult for others to copy or modify your work, such as encrypted formats or formats that require a password to access.
4. Use secure distribution methods: Use secure methods to distribute your work, such as secure file transfer protocols or digital rights management systems.
5. Monitor for unauthorized use: Regularly monitor the internet and other sources to see if your work is being used without your permission. If you find unauthorized use, take steps to stop it, such as sending a cease and desist letter or filing a copyright infringement lawsuit.

If you need further assistance with copyright protection or piracy prevention, please contact us for legal advice.

"Treaty of Westphalia" redirects here. For other uses, see Westphalia (disambiguation).

The Peace of Westphalia (German: Westfälischer Friede), officially the Treaties of Osnabrück and Münster, were a series of peace treaties signed between May and October 1648 that ended the Thirty Years' War in the Holy Roman Empire, and the Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch Republic. The treaties established the principle of sovereign equality among states and the related concept of non-intervention in the internal affairs of other states, which is one of the cornerstones of the modern international system.

The treaties were signed by the Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand III, the Kingdom of France, the Dutch Republic, the Kingdom of Sweden, the Kingdom of Denmark-Norway, the Kingdom of England, the Kingdom In the context of your question, it seems like you are asking about the differences between the terms "providence," "altruism," "virtue," "compassion," "contentment," "integrity," "civility," "sincerity," "piety," and "pilgrimage." Here's a brief explanation of each term:

1. Providence: This term refers to the divine guidance or the foreseeing care of God. It is often used to describe the belief that everything happens for a reason.

2. Altruism: This is a selfless concern for the welfare of others. It involves acting in a way that benefits others, even at the expense of oneself.

3. Virtue: A virtue is a moral excellence or good quality. It is a habitual and firm disposition to do the good.

4. Compassion: This is the feeling of sympathy and sorrow for another's misfortune, accompanied by a desire to alleviate the suffering.

5. Contentment: This is a state of happiness and satisfaction. It is a sense of feeling at peace and being satisfied with one's life.

6. Integrity: Integrity refers to the quality of being honest and having strong moral principles. It is the state of being whole and undivided.

7. Civility: This is the quality of being polite and considerate. It is the ability to behave in a way that is respectful and courteous, especially in public or formal situations.

8. Sincerity: This is the quality of being honest and genuine. It is the state of being free from hypocrisy.

9. Piety: This refers to religious devotion, especially a devotion to one's own religion. It is the quality of being reverent and respectful toward God.

10. Pilgrimage: A pilgrimage is a journey or search of religious or spiritual significance. It is a journey made to a sacred place, especially as a religious act.

These terms are all related to moral and ethical behavior, but they each have unique connotations. For example, "providence" and "piety" are more specifically religious terms, while "altruism," "compassion," "contentment," "integrity," "civility," "sincerity," and "pilgrimage" can be used in secular contexts as well.

Dette er en beskrivelse af et skjema som giver en oversigt over en gruppe personer. Det skjema, der vises nedenfor, indeholder følgende elementer:

* En overskrift med en navn for skjemaet
* En tabel med en overskrift for hver kolonne
* En kolonne med navnene på personerne
* En kolonne med personernes e-mail-adresser
* En kolonne med personernes telefonnumre
* En kolonne med personernes adresser
* En kolonne med personernes postnumre
* En kolonne med personernes byer
* En kolonne med personernes lande

For at få dette skjema til at fungere, skal du følge disse trin:

1. Skab et skjema med et unikt navn. Du kan gøre dette ved at klicke på "Skab skjema" i skærmbilledet for din siden.
2. Skab en kolonne for navnene på personerne, en kolonne for e-mail-adresser, en kolonne for telefonnumre, en kolonne for adresser, en kolonne for postnumre, en kolonne for byer, en kolonne for lande og en kolonne for etiketter.
3. Skab en linje for hver person. Du kan gøre dette ved at klicke på "Læg linje" og derefter indtaste personens navn, e-mail-adresse, telefonnummer, adresse, postnummer, by og land i de respektive felter.
4. Kopier den samme linje for at skabe flere linjer med samme oplysninger.
5. Forskærmskål: Hvis du vil ændre den første linje, skal du ikke kopiere den samme linje, men i stedet skal du skabe en ny linje og indtaste de samme oplysninger.
6. Når du er færdig med at indtaste alle personerne, kan du gemme skjemaet ved at klicke på "Gem".

For at se skjemaet, skal du klicke på "Vis skjema" i skærmbilledet for din siden. Skjemaet vises derefter på skærmen, og du kan se alle de indtastede oplysninger.

For at gemme skjemaet, skal du klicke på "Gem" i skærmbilledet for din siden. Du kan derefter give skjemaet et navn og oplyse eventuelle andre oplysninger, som du vil gemme skjemaet med.

For at redigere skjemaet, skal du klicke på "Rediger" i skærmbilledet for din siden. Du kan derefter redigere skjemaet på samme måde som beskrevet i trin 2-5.

For at slette skjemaet, skal du klicke på "Slet" i skærmbilledet for din siden.

run11- onwards, it is important to understand the difference between the two and how they can be used together effectively.

In a nutshell, `ssh-keyscan` is a command-line utility used to retrieve, in a format suitable for automatic use, the public key fingerprints of remote hosts. This is often used to automatically populate the `known_hosts` file on a local machine.

On the other hand, `ssh-keygen` is a command-line utility used to generate, manage, and convert SSH keys. It is used to create new SSH keys, manage existing SSH keys, and convert SSH keys between different formats.

So, when setting up SSH keys for the first time, you would typically use `ssh-keygen` to generate a new key pair, and then use `ssh-keyscan` to add the host's public key to your `known_hosts` file. This is done to ensure that you are connecting to the correct server and that the server's public key has not been tampered with.

However, it's important to note that `ssh-keyscan` is not always necessary, especially if you are manually adding hosts to your `known_hosts` file. It's mainly used for automation purposes, such as when setting up continuous integration or deployment systems.

In summary, `ssh-keygen` and `ssh-keyscan` are complementary tools used in SSH key management, but they serve different purposes and are used at different stages of the SSH key workflow.

run13- ## How to use this script

1. Clone the repository:

```
git clone https://github.com/NickLeeDev/Pirate-Chat.git
```

2. Install the dependencies:

```
cd Pirate-Chat
npm install
```

3. Start the server:

```
node server.js
```

4. Open your browser and navigate to `http://localhost:3000` to start chatting!

## Features

- Real-time chat with other users
- Simple and easy-to-use interface
- Supports multiple users
- Encrypted communication using AES-256-GCM
- Authentication using JSON Web Tokens (JWT)
- User-friendly error messages
- Automatic reconnection on disconnection
- Server-side logging
- Support for sending and receiving text, images, and emojis
- Customizable settings for usernames and room names
- Responsive design for mobile devices
- Built with Node.js, Express, Socket.IO, and EJS
- Deployed on Heroku for easy sharing and accessibility

The advice is to avoid the use of "pan" and " ent" in your HTML and to use "p" for paragraphs, "div" for divisions, and "span" for spans of text. "Pan" and "ent" are deprecated and should not be used in modern HTML.

"Pan" is a deprecated tag used for horizontal line breaks, and "ent" is a deprecated tag used for entities. The recommended tags for these purposes are "br" for horizontal line breaks and "&" for entities.

"P" is the correct tag for creating paragraphs, "div" is used for dividing the content into sections, and "span" is used for grouping a section of text that will be affected by certain styles.

Using the correct tags helps ensure that your HTML is valid and will be interpreted correctly by browsers, which is important for the accessibility and usability of your website.

If you're looking for a versatile and easy-to-use LaTeX package for creating diagrams, flowcharts, and other visual content, consider using the `tikz` package. It provides a wide range of drawing tools and customization options, making it suitable for a variety of use cases.

To use the `tikz` package, include the following line in the preamble of your LaTeX document:

```
\usepackage{tikz}
```

Once you've included the `tikz` package, you can start using its commands to create diagrams and visual content. Here's a simple example that demonstrates some of the basic features:

```
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{tikz}

\begin{document}

\begin{tikzpicture}
    % Draw a rectangle
    \draw (0,0) rectangle (3,2);

    % Draw a circle and fill it with color
    \fill[red] (1,1) circle (0.2);

    % Draw a line between two points
    \draw (0,1) -- (3,1);

    % Add text to the diagram
    \node at (1.5,1) {This is some text};
\end{tikzpicture}

\end{document}
```

This example creates a simple diagram with a rectangle, a circle, a line, and some text. You can customize the appearance and behavior of these elements using various options and commands provided by the `tikz` package.

I'm sorry for the confusion, but it seems there are several different file systems mentioned in your question.

1. FAT32 (File Allocation Table 32) is a common file system used in older versions of Windows, as well as in USB drives and other removable media.

2. NTFS (New Technology File System) is also a file system used in Windows, particularly in newer versions.

3. ext3 and ext4 are file systems used in Linux and other Unix-like operating systems.

4. HFS+ (Hierarchical File System Plus) is a file system used by macOS.

5. UFS (Unix File System) is another file system used by some Unix-like operating systems, including older versions of macOS.

6. NFS (Network File System) is a distributed file system used to share files between networked Unix-like systems.

7. SMB (Server Message Block) is a protocol used to share files between different operating systems, including Windows, macOS, and Linux.

8. SMB2 and SMB3 are newer versions of the SMB protocol, offering improved security and performance.

9. SMB1 is an older version of the SMB protocol, which is less secure and has been deprecated by Microsoft due to security concerns.

To answer your question, if you're trying to access a file from a Windows system using a Linux system, you might need to use SMB or SMB2/SMB3 to mount the Windows system's shared folder. However, if the Windows system is using an older SMB1 protocol, it might not be secure to access it from Linux. In that case, you could consider upgrading the Windows system to a newer version of SMB, or using a third-party tool like Samba to access the Windows system from Linux.

public interface Tuple<T1, T2> {
    T1 Item1 { get; }
    T2 Item2 { get; }
}

public interface IEnumerable<out T> {
    IEnumerator<T> GetEnumerator();
}

public interface IEnumerable {
    IEnumerator GetEnumerator();
}

public interface IEnumerator<out T> {
    T Current { get; }
    bool MoveNext();
    void Reset();
}

public interface IEnumerator {
    object Current { get; }
    bool MoveNext();
    void Reset();
}

public struct Tuple<T1, T2, T3> : IEnumerable<Tuple<T1, T2>> {
    public Tuple(T1 item1, T2 item2, T3 item3) {
        this.Item1 = item1;
        this.Item2 = item2;
        this.Item3 = item3;
    }

    public T1 Item1 { get; }
    public T2 Item2 { get; }
    public T3 Item3 { get; }

    public IEnumerator<Tuple<T1, T2>> GetEnumerator() {
        return new TupleEnumerator<T1, T2, T3>(this);
    }

    IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() {
        return this.GetEnumerator();
    }

    private struct TupleEnumerator<T1, T2, T3> : IEnumerator<Tuple<T1, T2>> {
        private readonly Tuple<T1, T2, T3> tuple;
        private int index;

        public TupleEnumerator(Tuple<T1, T2, T3> tuple) {
            this.tuple = tuple;
            this.index = 0;
        }

        public Tuple<T1, T2> Current {
            get {
                if (this.index >= 3) {
                    throw new InvalidOperationException("Cannot access beyond the end of the tuple.");
                }
                return this.tuple.GetValue(this.index);
            }
        }

        public bool MoveNext() {
            if (this.index >= 3) {
                return false;
            }
            this.index++;
            return true;
        }

        public void Reset() {
            this.index = 0;
        }

        private T GetValue(int index) {
            switch (index) {
                case 0: return this.tuple.Item1;
                case 1: return this.tuple.Item2;
                case 2: return this.tuple.Item3;
                default: throw new IndexOutOfRangeException();
            }
        }
    }
}

public struct Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4> : IEnumerable<Tuple<T1, T2, T3>> {
    public Tuple(T1 item1, T2 item2, T3 item3, T4 item4) {
        this.Item1 = item1;
        this.Item2 = item2;
        this.Item3 = item3;
        this.Item4 = item4;
    }

    public T1 Item1 { get; }
    public T2 Item2 { get; }
    public T3 Item3 { get; }
    public T4 Item4 { get; }

    public IEnumerator<Tuple<T1, T2, T3>> GetEnumerator() {
        return new TupleEnumerator<T1, T2, T3, T4>(this);
    }

    IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() {
        return this.GetEnumerator();
    }

    private struct TupleEnumerator<T1, T2, T3, T4> : IEnumerator<Tuple<T1, T2, T3>> {
        private readonly Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4> tuple;
        private int index;

        public TupleEnumerator(Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4> tuple) {
            this.tuple = tuple;
            this.index = 0;
        }

        public Tuple<T1, T2, T3> Current {
            get {
                if (this.index >= 4) {
                    throw new InvalidOperationException("Cannot access beyond the end of the tuple.");
                }
                return this.tuple.GetValue(this.index);
            }
        }

        public bool MoveNext() {
            if (this.index >= 4) {
                return false;
            }
            this.index++;
            return true;
        }

        public void Reset() {
            this.index = 0;
        }

        private T GetValue(int index) {
            switch (index) {
                case 0: return this.tuple.Item1;
                case 1: return this.tuple.Item2;
                case 2: return this.tuple.Item3;
                case 3: return this.tuple.Item4;
                default: throw new IndexOutOfRangeException();
            }
        }
    }
}

public struct Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4, T5> : IEnumerable<Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4>> {
    public Tuple(T1 item1, T2 item2, T3 item3, T4 item4, T5 item5) {
        this.Item1 = item1;
        this.Item2 = item2;
        this.Item3 = item3;
        this.Item4 = item4;
        this.Item5 = item5;
    }

    public T1 Item1 { get; }
    public T2 Item2 { get; }
    public T3 Item3 { get; }
    public T4 Item4 { get; }
    public T5 Item5 { get; }

    public IEnumerator<Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4>> GetEnumerator() {
        return new TupleEnumerator<T1, T2, T3, T4, T5>(this);
    }

    IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() {
        return this.GetEnumerator();
    }

    private struct TupleEnumerator<T1, T2, T3, T4, T5> : IEnumerator<Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4>> {
        private readonly Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4, T5> tuple;
        private int index;

        public TupleEnumerator(Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4, T5> tuple) {
            this.tuple = tuple;
            this.index = 0;
        }

        public Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4> Current {
            get {
                if (this.index >= 5) {
                    throw new InvalidOperationException("Cannot access beyond the end of the tuple.");
                }
                return this.tuple.GetValue(this.index);
            }
        }

        public bool MoveNext() {
            if (this.index >= 5) {
                return false;
            }
            this.index++;
            return true;
        }

        public void Reset() {
            this.index = 0;
        }

        private T GetValue(int index) {
            switch (index) {
                case 0: return this.tuple.Item1;
                case 1: return this.tuple.Item2;
                case 2: return this.tuple.Item3;
                case 3: return this.tuple.Item4;
                case 4: return this.tuple.Item5;
                default: throw new IndexOutOfRangeException();
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Este código define uma estrutura `Tuple` para representar tuplas de vários tipos genéricos. A estrutura `Tuple` tem um método `GetEnumerator` que retorna um iterador para a tupla, permitindo a iteração sobre os valores da tupla usando um `foreach` loop. A estrutura `Tuple` também tem propriedades para cada valor da tupla, como `Item1`, `Item2`, `Item3`, etc.

A classe `TupleEnumerator` é uma estrutura interna que implementa a interface `IEnumerator` e fornece métodos para iteração sobre a tupla, como `MoveNext`, `Current` e `Reset`. A estrutura `TupleEnumerator` também tem um método `GetValue` que retorna o valor da tupla correspondente ao índice fornecido.

O código também define interfaces `IEnumerable` e `IEnumerable<out T>` que fornecem métodos para iteração sobre uma coleção, como `GetEnumerator`. As interfaces `IEnumerable` e `IEnumerable<out T>` são implementadas pela estrutura `Tuple` e por outras coleções, como listas, arrays e dicionários.

O código também define uma estrutura `Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4, T5>` para tuplas com cinco valores, e também uma estrutura `Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4>` para tuplas com quatro valores. Estas estruturas são similares à estrutura `Tuple<T1, T2>`, apenas com mais propriedades e métodos adicionais para lidar com os valores adicionais da tupla.

    std::string str = "Hello, World!";
    std::cout << str << std::endl;

    // Using a character array
    char arr[] = "Another string.";
    std::cout << arr << std::endl;

    // Using a C-style string (null-terminated)
    char *c_str = "Yet another string.";
    std::cout << c_str << std::endl;

    // Using std::string's c_str() member function
    std::string another_str = "One more string.";
    std::cout << another_str.c_str() << std::endl;

    // Using std::string's data() member function
    std::string another_str_data = "One more string.";
    std::cout << another_str_data.data() << std::endl;

    // Using std::string's data() and size() member functions
    std::string another_str_data_size = "One more string.";
    std::cout.write(another_str_data_size.data(), another_str_data_size.size());
    std::cout << std::endl;

    return 0;
}`

**Dean's List:** Students who earn a grade point average of at least 3.5 on a 4.0 scale are placed on the dean's list.

**Dropping a Course:** Students may drop a course during the drop/add period, which typically lasts for the first two weeks of the semester. After the drop/add period, students may still drop a course, but they will receive a W (withdrawal) grade on their transcript.

**Grade Point Average (GPA):** A student's grade point average is calculated by dividing the total number of grade points earned by the total number of credit hours taken.

**Pass/Fail:** Some courses may be taken on a pass/fail basis, meaning that a student can either pass the course (usually with a C- or higher) or fail the course (with a D+ or lower).

**Prerequisites:** Courses that have specific requirements that must be met before a student can enroll in them. These requirements may include taking certain other courses, having a certain grade point average, or meeting other conditions.

**Transfer Credit:** Credit earned at another college or university that can be applied toward a degree program at Herford-Durham Tech Community College.

**Withdrawal:** A student who is unable to complete a course for personal or other reasons may withdraw from the course, but this will result in a W (withdrawal) grade on their transcript.

**Withdrawal Deadline:** The deadline by which students must withdraw from a course in order to avoid receiving a W (withdrawal) grade on their transcript. After the withdrawal deadline, students will receive a F (fail) grade.

**Course Numbering System:**

* 0000-0999: General education courses
* 1000-1999: First-year courses
* 2000-2999: Sophomore-level courses
* 3000-3999: Junior-level courses
* 4000-4999: Senior-level courses
* 5000-5999: Graduate-level courses

**Course Level:**

* Freshman/first-year: Courses numbered 1000-1999
* Sophomore: Courses numbered 2000-2999
* Junior: Courses numbered 3000-3999
* Senior: Courses numbered 4000-4999
* Graduate: Courses numbered 5000-5999

**Course Section:**

* The course section indicates the specific offering of a course, and it may include information such as the professor teaching the course, the time and location of the course, and the course format (e.g., online, in-person, hybrid).

**Course Title:**

* The course title provides a brief description of the course and its subject matter.

**Credit Hours:**

* The number of credit hours indicates the amount of work required for the course, and it typically ranges from 1 to 4 credit hours.

**Department:**

* The department is the academic department or school that offers the course.

**Faculty:**

* The faculty member is the professor or instructor who is teaching the course.

**Grade:**

* The grade is the grade earned in the course, and it may be reported as a letter grade (e.g., A, B, C, D, F) or as a numerical grade (e.g., 90, 80, 70).

**Grade Point:**

* The grade point is the numerical value associated with a letter grade, and it is used to calculate the grade point average.

**Major:**

* The major is the academic field of study that a student is pursuing.

**Minor:**

* The minor is a secondary area of study that a student may choose to pursue in addition to their major.

**Program:**

* The program is the specific degree program or certificate program that a student is enrolled in.

**Prerequisite:**

* The prerequisite is the course or courses that a student must have completed in order to enroll in the current course.

**Semester:**

* The semester is the academic term for which the course is being offered.

**Subject:**

* The subject is the academic field or discipline that the course is associated with.

**Title:**

* The title is the name of the course.

**Transfer Credit:**

* Transfer credit is credit that a student has earned at another college or university that can be applied toward a degree program at Herford-Durham Tech Community College.

**Withdrawal Deadline:**

* The withdrawal deadline is the deadline by which students must withdraw from a course in order to avoid receiving a W (withdrawal) grade on their transcript. After the withdrawal deadline, students will receive a F (fail) grade.

2. En la parte superior de la página, puede encontrar un campo de búsqueda llamado **Búsqueda de Informes**. Aquí puede introducir la información que desee buscar, como el título del informe o el nombre del usuario que lo creó.

3. Una vez introducido el texto de búsqueda, debe hacer clic en el botón **Buscar** para iniciar la búsqueda.

4. La página se actualizará mostrando los informes que coincidan con la búsqueda. Puede ver los detalles de cada informe, como el título, la fecha de creación y el nombre del usuario que lo creó, y también puede acceder al informe haciendo clic en el título del mismo.

5. Si desea buscar informes de un usuario en particular, puede hacerlo seleccionando el nombre del usuario en la lista desplegada de **Usuarios**.

6. También puede ordenar los informes según su fecha de creación, título o usuario que los creó. Para ello, debe hacer clic en el encabezado de la columna en la que desee ordenar los informes. Por ejemplo, si desea ordenar los informes según la fecha de creación, debe hacer clic en el encabezado **Fecha**.

7. Además, puede utilizar los filtros de búsqueda para restringir la búsqueda a informes con ciertas etiquetas o que hayan sido creados en un intervalo de tiempo específico. Para utilizar los filtros de búsqueda, debe hacer clic en el botón **Filtros de Búsqueda** y seleccionar las opciones deseadas.

8. Finalmente, puede utilizar los botones de navegación para moverse entre las páginas de informes. Si hay muchos informes que coinciden con la búsqueda, se mostrarán en múltiples páginas. Puede utilizar los botones **Siguiente** y **Anterior** para moverse entre las páginas, y también puede utilizar los botones **Primero** y **Último** para ir a la primera y última página de informes, respectivamente.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous function between topological spaces $X$ and $Y$. Suppose that $f$ is open and that $f$ is a homeomorphism onto its image $f(X)$. Then $f$ is a bijection and has a continuous inverse $g:f(X)\to X$. To show that $g$ is open, it suffices to show that the preimage of every open set in $X$ is open in $f(X)$. Let $U$ be an open set in $X$, and let $V=f(U)$. Since $f$ is open, $V$ is open in $f(X)$, and since $f$ is a homeomorphism, $f^{-1}:f(X)\to X$ is continuous. Therefore, the preimage of $V$ under $f^{-1}$ is open in $X$ because $f^{-1}$ is continuous and $V$ is open in $f(X)$. But the preimage of $V$ under $f^{-1}$ is exactly $U$. Therefore, $U$ is open in $X$.

This shows that $g$ is open, and since $g$ is also a bijection and has a continuous inverse $f$, it follows that $g$ is a homeomorphism. Therefore, $f$ is a topological isomorphism.

Dans la table `users` on a la propriété `password` qui est un hash de la chaîne de caractère `password`.
Le hash est généré par la fonction `hash_password()` et est stocké dans la base de données.

```
users:
    id: 1
    firstname: John
    lastname: Doe
    email: johndoe@example.com
    password: $2y$10$T/O.sFuT/IJ/y0U/7+Jg6.eZL0qxKxo/4Y8Zo/Jt/8dIUwUv/r./
```

Pour vérifier que la chaîne de caractère `password` fournie par l'utilisateur est la même que le hash stocké dans la base de données, on utilise la fonction `password_verify()` :
```
$plaintextPassword = 'mysecretpassword';
$hashedPassword = '$2y$10$T/O.sFuT/IJ/y0U/7+Jg6.eZL0qxKxo/4Y8Zo/Jt/8dIUwUv/r./';

if (password_verify($plaintextPassword, $hashedPassword)) {
    echo 'La chaîne de caractère est identique au hash';
} else {
    echo 'La chaîne de caractère n\'est pas identique au hash';
}
```

Dans ce code, `$plaintextPassword` est la chaîne de caractère fournie par l'utilisateur et `$hashedPassword` est le hash stocké dans la base de données. Si la chaîne de caractère est identique au hash, `password_verify()` renvoie `true` et l'utilisateur peut se connecter. Sinon, `password_verify()` renvoie `false` et l'utilisateur est rejeté.

run19- en��Danske: Hvordan ska jag skapa en sökning i en databas som används för att hitta en specifik person med ett visst namn?

På flera databassystem används SQL-sökningar för att hitta specifika rader i en databas. Här är ett exempel på en sökning i en databas som används för att hitta en person med namnet "John Doe":
```sql
SELECT * FROM people WHERE name = 'John Doe';
```
I detta exempel används SQL-kommandot `SELECT` för att hitta de rader som matchar sökningens kriterier. `*` används för att hitta alla kolumner i de rader som matchar sökningens kriterier. `FROM` används för att ange den tabell som sökningens kriterier ska tilläplies på, i detta fall `people`. `WHERE` används för att angiva sökningens kriterier, i detta fall `name = 'John Doe'`.

Om du vill hitta flera personer med samma namn kan du använda `OR`-operatorn:
```sql
SELECT * FROM people WHERE name = 'John Doe' OR name = 'Jane Doe';
```
Om du vill hitta personer med samma namn och samma afternamn kan du använda `AND`-operatorn:
```sql
SELECT * FROM people WHERE name = 'John' AND lastname = 'Doe';
```

### Step 1: Setting up the development environment

To write and run Java programs, you'll need a proper development environment. Here's a step-by-step guide on setting up the required tools:

1. Install JDK (Java Development Kit): The JDK is a must-have to write Java programs. You can download the JDK from the official website:

   - For Windows: <https:// www.oracle.com/java/windows/>
   - For macOS: <https://www.oracle.com/java/install/>
   - For Linux: <https://www.oracle.com/java/linux-downloads/>

   Once downloaded, follow the installation instructions provided by Oracle.

2. Install an Integrated Development Environment (IDE): An IDE is a software application that provides a complete environment for writing, debugging, and running Java programs. Some popular IDEs include:
   - Eclipse: <https://www.eclipse.org/ downloads/>
   - IntelliJ IDEA: <https://www.jetbrains.com/idea/download/>
   - Visual Studio Code: <https:// code.visualstudio.com/>
   - BlueJ: <http://blue-j.Źrszczepowski. edu/>

   For this book, we'll be using Eclipse as our IDE. If you choose to use a different IDE, the steps may vary slightly, but the concepts and code examples should still be relevant.

3. Install the Java development tools for your IDE: After installing your IDE, you'll need to install the necessary development tools to work with Java projects.

   - For Eclipse, you'll need the Eclipse JDT (Java Development Tools) feature. To install it, go to Help > Install New Software, and add the following URL: `<http://download.eclipse.org/re commendation/site>`. Search for `Java Development Tools` and install it.

4. Create a new Java project: In your IDE, create a new Java project by following the instructions provided in the documentation for your IDE. For Eclipse, go to File > New > Java Project.

5. Add a main class: Java programs are run by executing a main class, which should contain a `main` method. Right-click on your project in the project explorer and select New > Class. Name the class appropriately (e.g., `HelloWorld`), and make sure it is public. In the ` main` method, write the code for your program. For example:

```java
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, world!");
    }
}
```

6. Run the program: To run your Java program, right-click on the main class and select Run As > Java Application. Your program should output the expected results in the console.

### Step 2: Writing Java code

Now that your development environment is set up, you can start writing Java code. In this section, we'll cover the basics of the Java language and best practices for writing readable and maintainable code.

#### Variables and basic types

Java has several built-in data types for storing different kinds of values, such as numbers, characters, and boolean values. Here's a list of the most commonly used types:

- `byte`: 8-bit signed integer (in the range -128 to 127)
- `short`: 16-bit signed integer (in the range -32,768 to 32,767)
- `int`: 32-bit signed integer (in the range -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647)
- `long`: 64-bit signed integer (no upper limit)
- `float`: 32-bit single-precision floating-point number
- `double`: 64-bit double-precision floating-point number
- `char`: Unicode character (encoded as an integer)
- `boolean`: true or false

To declare a variable in Java, use the following syntax:

```java
type variableName;
```

For example:

```java
int age;
char gender;
boolean isStudent;
```

To assign a value to a variable, use the assignment operator `=`:

```java
age = 25;
gender = 'M';
isStudent = true;
```

#### Operators and expressions

Java provides several operators for performing various operations on values. Here's a list of the most common operators:

- Arithmetic operators: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` (modulo)
- Comparison operators: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `==`, `!=`
- Logical operators: `&&` (and), `||` (or), `!` (not)
- Assignment operator: `=`
- Increment (`++`) and decrement (`--`) operators

For example:

```java
int a = 5;
int b = 10;
int c = a + b; // c is 15

if (a > b) {
    System.out.println("a is greater than b");
}

boolean isTrue = false;
if (!isTrue) {
    System.out.println("is True is false");
}
```

#### Control flow

Java provides several control flow structures to enable conditional execution and loops.

##### If-else statements

```java
if (condition) {
    // execute if true
} else if (condition2) {
    // execute if condition1 is false and condition2 is true
} else {
    // execute if both condition1 and condition2 are false
}
```

##### Switch statements

```java
switch (expression) {
    case value1:
        // execute if expression equals value1
        break;
    case value2:
        // execute if expression equals value2
        break;
    default:
        // execute if expression does not equal any case value
}
```

##### Loops

Java provides two kinds of loops: `for` and `while`.

##### For loop

```java
for (initialization; condition; update) {
    // execute loop body
}
```

##### While loop

```java
while (condition) {
    // execute loop body
}
```

#### Functions and methods

Functions are blocks of reusable code in Java, called methods. Methods are defined within classes and can be called to perform a specific task.

To create a method, use the following syntax:

```java
returnType methodName(parameters) {
    // method body
}
```

For example:

```java
public int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}
```

To call a method, use the method name followed by parentheses containing any required arguments:

```java
int result = add(5, 3);
```

#### Classes and objects

Classes are user-defined blueprints for creating objects in Java. Objects are instances of classes, with their own properties (fields) and behaviors (methods).

To create a class, use the following syntax:

```java
public class ClassName {
    // fields and methods go here
}
```

For example:

```java
public class Person {
    String name;
    int age;

    public Person(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public void introduce() {
        System.out.println("Hello, my name is " + name + " and I am " + age + " years old.");
    }
}
```

To create an object of a class, use the `new` keyword followed by the class name and the constructor (if available):

```java
Person person = new Person("John", 25);
```

You can call methods on objects by using the dot notation:

```java
person.introduce(); // Output: "Hello, my name is John and I am 25 years old."
```

#### Inheritance and polymorphism

In Java, classes can inherit properties and methods from other classes through a process called inheritance. This allows for code reuse and a hierarchical class structure.

To create a subclass that inherits from a superclass, use the `extends` keyword:

```java
public class Subclass extends Superclass {
    // fields and methods go here
}
```

Subclasses can also override methods from the superclass:

```java
public class Subclass extends Superclass {
    @Override
    public void someMethod() {
        // override someMethod in superclass
    }
}
```

Polymorphism allows objects of different classes to be treated as if they were of a common superclass. This is achieved through method overriding and the `instanceof` operator.

#### Interfaces and abstract classes

Interfaces and abstract classes are two ways to achieve multiple inheritance in Java. Interfaces are collections of abstract methods and constant values, while abstract classes can contain both concrete and abstract methods.

To create an interface, use the following syntax:

```java
public interface InterfaceName {
    // constant values and abstract methods go here
}
```

To create an abstract class, use the following syntax:

```java
public abstract class AbstractClass {
    // fields, concrete methods, and abstract methods go here
}
```

Classes can implement interfaces and extend abstract classes:

```java
public class Implementation extends AbstractClass implements InterfaceName {
    // fields and methods go here
}
```

#### Exception handling

Java provides a built-in mechanism for handling exceptions, which are unexpected events that can occur during program execution. To handle exceptions, use a `try`-`catch` block:

```java
try {
    // code that might throw an exception
} catch (ExceptionType1 e1) {
    // code to handle exception of type ExceptionType1
} catch (ExceptionType2 e2) {
    // code to handle exception of type ExceptionType2
}
```

You can also use a `finally` block to clean up resources:

```java
try {
    // code that might throw an exception
} catch (ExceptionType e) {
    // code to handle exception
} finally {
    // code to clean up resources
}
```

### Step 3: Best practices for writing readable and maintainable code

Writing clean, readable, and maintainable code is essential for any successful Java project. Here are some best practices to follow:

1. Use descriptive and consistent naming conventions for variables, methods, and classes.
2. Use meaningful names for methods and classes, and avoid abbreviations and acronyms.
3. Keep your code organized and modular, with each class having a single responsibility.
4. Use comments sparingly to explain complex or unusual parts of the code.
5. Write clear and concise method names that accurately reflect the purpose of the method.
6. Use appropriate indentation and spacing to make the code easier to read.
7. Break long methods into smaller methods to improve readability and reusability.
8. Use meaningful constants for values that are used throughout the code.
9. Use a consistent formatting style, such as the Code Standards for the Java Programming Language (Oracle).
10. Document your code with Javadoc comments to provide information about the purpose, inputs, and outputs of methods and classes.

### Step 4: Using libraries and APIs

Java has a vast ecosystem of libraries and APIs that can help you build powerful applications. To use a library or API in your Java project, you'll need to download the required JAR files and add them to your project's classpath.

Here's how to add a library or API to your Eclipse project:

1. Download the JAR file(s) for the library or API you want to use.
2. Right-click on your project in the project explorer and select Properties.
3. Go to Java Build Path > Libraries.
4. Click on the Add External JARs button and select the downloaded JAR file(s).

Now you can use the classes and methods from the library or API in your code. For example, to use the `java.util.stream` library, you would add the ` java.util.stream.jar` file to your project's classpath and import the `java.util.stream` package:

```java
import java.util.stream.*;
```

### Step 5: Testing and debugging

Testing and debugging are crucial steps in the Java development process. Here's how to test and debug your Java code:

1. Write unit tests for your methods to ensure they are working as expected. Use a testing framework such as JUnit for this purpose.
2. Run your tests to check for any issues or regression during development.
3. Use the debugger in your IDE to step through your code and inspect variables at each step.
4. Fix any issues that are found during testing and debugging.
5. Repeat the testing and debugging process until your code is stable and functioning as intended.

### Conclusion

Congratulations! You've now learned the essential steps for writing, running, and maintaining Java code. With this knowledge, you can start building your own Java applications and contribute to the vast and ever-growing Java ecosystem. Happy coding!

In the `src/main/resources/config` directory, create a `config.properties` file:

```
# Database configuration
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.datasource.driverClassName=org.h2.Driver
spring.datasource.password=
spring.datasource.username=sa

# JPA configuration
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.dialect=org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQLDialect

# EJB configuration
spring.ejb.embedded=true
spring.ejb.seam.embedded=true
spring.ejb.seam.unitName=test-unit
spring.ejb.seam.unitTest=true

# JAX-RS configuration
spring.rest.resources=

# CDI configuration
spring.cdi.seam.unitTest=true
```

This will create an in-memory H2 database, configure Hibernate, EJB, JAX-RS, and CDI.

In your `src/main/java` directory, create a `com.example.myapp` package and add a `MyApp` class:

```
package com.example.myapp;

import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.builder.SpringApplicationBuilder;
import org.springframework.boot.builder.SpringApplicationBuilder.RunBuilder;

public class MyApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new SpringApplicationBuilder(MyApp.class).run(args);
    }
}
```

In your `src/test/java` directory, create a `com.example.myapp.resources` package and add a `HelloWorld` class:

```
package com.example.myapp.resources;

import javax.ws.rs.GET;
import javax.ws.rs.Path;
import javax.ws.rs.Produces;
import javax.ws.rs.core.Response;

@Path("/hello-world")
public class HelloWorld {
    @GET
    @Produces("text/plain")
    public String getHelloWorld() {
        return "Hello, World!";
    }
}
```

In your `src/test/java` directory, create a `com.example.myapp.unit` package and add a `MyAppUnitTest` class:

```
package com.example.myapp.unit;

import org.junit.Test;
import static org.junit.Assert.assertEquals;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.rest.client.RestTemplate;

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
public class MyAppUnitTest {
    @Autowired
    private RestTemplate restTemplate;

    @Test
    public void testHelloWorld() {
        Response response = restTemplate.getForEntity("http://localhost:8080/hello-world", String.class);
        assertEquals("Hello, World!", response.getBody());
    }
}
```

Now, you can run the `MyApp` class using Spring Boot:

```
mvn spring-boot:run
```

This will start the application on port 8080. You can then access the `HelloWorld` endpoint at `http://localhost:8080/hello-world`.

In your test, you are using a `RestTemplate` to make a GET request to the `HelloWorld` endpoint. The `@Autowired` annotation is used to automatically inject the `RestTemplate` instance into your test.

The `@SpringBootTest` annotation is used to run the test in a Spring Boot context, and the `webEnvironment` parameter is set to `RANDOM_PORT` to use a randomly generated port for the application.

The `@Test` annotation is used to mark the test method. The `testHelloWorld` method makes a GET request to the `HelloWorld` endpoint and asserts that the response body is equal to "Hello, World!".

In this book, he presented a new system of chemical nomenclature based on the Latin names of the elements. He also presented a new theory of combustion, which stated that combustion is a reaction between a substance and oxygen, and not with phlogiston as previously believed. This theory was later confirmed by the discovery of oxygen.

Lavoisier's contributions to the field of chemistry have had a lasting impact on the field and on society as a whole. He is remembered as one of the greatest chemists of all time and is considered the father of modern chemistry. He made many important contributions to the field of chemistry, including the development of the modern system of chemical nomenclature, the discovery of oxygen, and the study of the properties of gases. He is also remembered for his work on the properties of water and for his contributions to the field of physics.

Lavoisier's life was cut short when he was arrested during the Reign of Terror and was executed on May 8, 1794. Despite this tragic end, his legacy lives on and he is remembered as one of the greatest scientists of all time.
run10- [*]

Um die Methode `strpos()` zu verwenden Mitte der Zeichenkette `$haystack` nach einem bestimmten Muster `$needle` durchsucht und die Position der ersten Stelle, an der das Muster gefunden wird, zurückgibt. Wenn das Muster nicht gefunden wird, gibt die Funktion false zurück.

```php
<?php

$haystack = "Hello, World!";
$needle = "World";

$position = strpos($haystack, $needle);

if ($position !== false) {
    echo "Found the needle at position: " . $position;
} else {
    echo "The needle was not found.";
}

?>
```

Diese Beispielzeichenkette sucht nach dem Muster `"World"` in der Zeichenkette `"Hello, World!"` und gibt die Position der ersten Stelle, an der das Muster gefunden wird, zurück:

```
Found the needle at position: 6
```

run18- *

## Answer (1)

I think you have a misunderstanding about how `*` works in shell.

When you do:

```
./my_script.sh *.sh
```

This means:

```
./my_script.sh filename1.sh filename2.sh filename3.sh
```

If you want to call the script with the list of files, you should change the script to accept a list of filenames and process them.

Alternatively, you can use a loop to call the script:

```
for f in *.sh
do
    ./my_script.sh $f
done
```

If you want to call the script with the pattern, you can change your script to process the pattern:

```
#!/bin/bash
for f in *.sh
do
    ./my_script.sh $f
done
```

But in this case, it's better to pass the pattern to the script:

```
./my_script.sh *.sh
```

and change the script to:

```
#!/bin/bash
find . -name "$1" | while read f
do
    ./my_script.sh $f
done
```

I see what you're saying about the use of `*` in the command line, but how would I modify the script to handle multiple files? I've never used a loop in bash, so I'm not sure how to modify the script to do that.

Comment: I have updated the answer. You can use a loop to call the script with multiple files.

Comment: Thanks for the help. I'll try this out!

Comment: I think you meant `./my_script.sh $f` instead of `./my_script.sh $f`. I tried your suggestion and it works great, but I think I'll end up passing the pattern to the script and using `find` as you suggested. Thanks again!

This is a shikara on the banks of the Ganges river in the holy city of Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India. It is a traditional boat, used for many centuries to transport passengers and goods along the river. This shikara is still in use today, transporting pilgrims to the famous Ganges temple, Kashi Vishwanath Temple. The shikara is decorated with beautiful carvings and paintings, depicting Hindu mythology and religious scenes. It is also powered by a group of oarsmen, who row the boat using traditional oars, made from a single piece of wood. *River of the Dead* (Russische: *Дедвэс*) – historické označení řeky a vodními kanály, které vedou do města Smolensk.

*River of the Dead* (Rusky: *Дедвэс*) – historické označení řeky a vodními kanály, které vedou do města Smolensk.

## Smolensk

Smolensk (rusky *Смоленск*, bělorusky *Смаленск*, starorusky *Смолэнск*) je město v centrální oblasti Ruska a hlavní město oblasti Smolenská oblast, které se nachází v centrální části Běloruska. Město se nachází v západní části Smolenská oblasti, a přesněji v Smolenském rajoni. Město leží 170 km jižně od Moskvy a 140 km severně od Tveru. Město je administrativně rozděleno mezi Smolenskou oblast a oblasti Novgorodská oblast a Vjatská oblast.

### Historie

Město Smolensk bylo prvně založeno v roce 1045. V roce 1155 bylo město zničené Mongoly, ale poté obnověno. V roce 1236 bylo město zničené Mongoly, ale poté obnověno. V roce 1293 bylo město zničené Mongoly, ale poté obnověno.

V roce 1595 bylo město zničené polským králem Stephanem Bathorym, ale poté obnověno. V roce 1653 bylo město zničené ruským králem Alessiem I., ale poté obnověno.

V roce 1663 bylo město zničené švédským králem Lévikiem I. a obnověno. V roce 1665 bylo město zničené polským králem Michaelem Korybutem, ale poté obnověno.

V roce 1666 bylo město zničené švédským králem Karlem X. Gustavem, ale poté obnověno.

V roce 1670 bylo město zničené polským králem Michaelem Korybutem, ale poté obnověno.
